issuing_body: European AI Office (Working Groups 2, 3, and 4 Chairs and Vice-Chairs)
covered_actors: Signatories (providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk)
SMEs and small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) providing general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
prohibited_practices: Proceeding with the development, making available on the market, or use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk when its systemic risks are not determined to be acceptable (Measure 4.2)

Training models on inputs or outputs from independent external evaluators' test runs without express permission, or taking legal or technical retaliation against independent external evaluators adhering to responsible disclosure rules (Measure 3.5, Appendix 3.5)
Retaliating in any form against persons providing information to competent authorities about systemic risks stemming from Signatories' models (Measure 8.3)

evidence.quote: Signatories commit to adopting a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework (“Framework”). The purpose of the Framework is to outline the systemic risk management processes and measures that Signatories implement to ensure the systemic risks stemming from their models are acceptable.

Signatories will implement a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process that involves four steps, without needing to duplicate parts of the model’s previous systemic risk assessments that are still appropriate:

Signatories will conduct at least state-of-the-art model evaluations in the modalities relevant to the systemic risk to assess the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects, as specified in Appendix 3.

Signatories will conduct such a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process at least before placing the model on the market and whenever the conditions specified in Measure 7.6, first and third paragraph, are met.

Signatories will ensure that the model evaluations assess the effectiveness of their safety mitigations at a breadth and depth appropriate for the extent to which systemic risk acceptance determination depends on the effectiveness of specific mitigations, including under adversarial pressure (e.g. finetuning attacks or jailbreaking).
(2) validation of network and physical access management and security gap identification, through (a) frequent red-teaming as appropriate to mitigate systemic risks;
(1) Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear: Risks from enabling chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) attacks or accidents.

Signatories commit to implementing appropriate processes and measures for keeping track of, documenting, and reporting to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, without undue delay relevant information about serious incidents along the entire model lifecycle and possible corrective measures to address them, as specified in the Measures of this Commitment.

Signatories will provide the information in points (1) to (7) of Measure 9.2 in an initial report that is submitted to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, at the following points in time, save in exceptional circumstances, if the involvement of their model (directly or indirectly) led to:

If and insofar as necessary to assess and/or mitigate systemic risks, Signatories will publish (e.g. via their websites) a summarised version of their Framework and Model Report(s), and updates thereof (pursuant to Commitments 1 and 7), with removals to not undermine the effectiveness of safety and/or security mitigations and to protect sensitive commercial information.

Signatories commit to reporting to the AI Office information about their model and their systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes and measures by creating a Safety and Security Model Report (“Model Report”) before placing a model on the market (as specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5).

Signatories will draw up and keep up-to-date the following information for the purpose of providing it to the AI Office upon request:
(1) a detailed description of the model’s architecture;

In addition to internal model evaluations, Signatories will ensure that adequately qualified independent external evaluators conduct model evaluations pursuant to this Appendix 3, with regards to the systemic risk, unless:

(1) independent external validation of security mitigation effectiveness if internal expertise is inadequate, through (a) regular independent external security reviews as appropriate to mitigate systemic risks;

Signatories commit to implementing an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for their models and their physical infrastructure along the entire model lifecycle, as specified in the Measures for this Commitment, to ensure the systemic risks stemming from their models that could arise from unauthorised releases, unauthorised access, and/or model theft are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).
Signatories will protect unreleased model parameters by implementing security mitigations that achieve the following mitigation objectives:

(9) implementing privacy-preserving logging and metadata analysis techniques of the model’s inputs and outputs using, e.g. watermarks, metadata, and/or other at least state-of-the-art provenance techniques;
(7) techniques to enable safe ecosystems of AI agents, such as model identifications, specialised communication protocols, or incident monitoring tools;
(3) reduction of the risk of model self-exfiltration, through (a) sandboxes around models, such as virtual machines and code execution isolation;
(4) reduction of the risk of sabotage to model training and use, through (a) checking training data for indications of tampering.
(1) filtering and cleaning training data, e.g. data that might result in undesirable model propensities such as unfaithful chain-of-thought traces;

A model is exempt from this Commitment if the model’s capabilities are inferior to the capabilities of at least one model for which the parameters are publicly available for download. Signatories will implement these security mitigations for a model until its parameters are made publicly available for download or securely deleted.

To serve as a guiding document for demonstrating compliance with the obligations provided for in Articles 53 and 55 AI Act, while recognising that adherence to the Code does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance with these obligations under the AI Act.
Signatories will provide the AI Office with (unredacted) access to their Framework, and updates thereof, within five business days of either being confirmed.

Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report (without redactions, unless they are required by national security laws to which Signatories are subject) by the time they place a model on the market, e.g. through a publicly accessible link or through a sufficiently secure channel specified by the AI Office.

To ensure providers of general-purpose AI models comply with their obligations under the AI Act and to enable the AI Office to assess compliance of providers of general-purpose AI models who choose to rely on the Code to demonstrate compliance with their obligations under the AI Act.
Further, Signatories will provide a sufficiently large number of random samples of inputs and outputs from a relevant model evaluation if subsequently asked by the AI Office;

compliance_deadlines: Safety and Security Framework confirmation: no later than 4 weeks after notifying the European Commission under Article 52(1) AI Act and no later than 2 weeks before placing the model on the market (Measure 1.1)
Framework and Framework update notifications to the AI Office: within 5 business days of confirmation (Measure 1.4)
Framework adequacy and adherence assessment: every 12 months from placing the model on the market, or sooner if materially undermined (Measure 1.3)

Safety and Security Model Report notification to the AI Office: by the time the model is placed on the market (delayable up to 15 business days with an interim report if acting in good faith); updates within 5 business days of confirmation; periodic updates at least every 6 months for most capable models unless exempted (Measures 7.6, 7.7)

Serious incident initial reports to the AI Office and national competent authorities: within 2 days for critical infrastructure disruption, 5 days for serious cybersecurity breach or model weight exfiltration, 10 days for death of a person, and 15 days for serious harm to health, fundamental rights infringement, or serious harm to property or the environment; intermediate reports at least every 4 weeks while unresolved; final report within 60 days after resolution (Measure 9.3)

Documentation retention: at least 5 years for serious incident documentation (Measure 9.4) and at least 10 years after placing the model on the market for additional technical documentation (Measure 10.1)
Responsible vulnerability disclosure embargo limit for independent external evaluators: maximum 30 business days unless exceptionally necessary (Measure 3.5)
Review of interface-access authorisations to unreleased model parameters: at least every 6 months (Appendix 4.3)
Remediation if a safe reference model loses its status: within 6 months (Appendix 2.2)
implementation_notes: Voluntary opt-in Code of Practice serving as a guiding document for Signatories (providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk) to demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55 of the EU AI Act, though adherence does not constitute conclusive evidence of legal compliance. Establishes 10 Commitments and 4 Appendices covering systemic risk management frameworks, specified systemic risks (CBRN, loss of control, cyber offence, harmful manipulation), state-of-the-art and independent external model evaluations, cybersecurity protections for unreleased model weights, governance and whistleblower protections, serious incident reporting, and public transparency. Provides proportionality and simplified compliance options for SMEs and SMCs, exemptions for 'similarly safe or safer' models, and exemptions from cybersecurity weight-protection commitments once model parameters are publicly available or inferior to publicly available models.
